newsitem.title: UK: ISO sees lower world 1996/97 sugar output, surplus.
newsitem.headline: ISO sees lower world 1996/97 sugar output, surplus.

text.p: World sugar production should reach 123.49 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, down on the 124.19 million posted in 1995/96, the International Sugar Organization (ISO) said on Friday.
The 1996/97 sugar surplus was expected to be sharply lower at 2.29 million tonnes, compared with 5.54 million in the previous crop year, ISO data showed.
World sugar consumption was expected to rise to 121.20 million tonnes in 1996/97 from 118.66 in 1995/96.
The ISO said only three countries had produced official data which had caused estimates to vary by more than 100,000 tonnes compared with February estimates.
Sugar production in the Philippines was now forecast at 1.86 million tonnes, 209,000 more than the previous forecast.
The estimate for South Korea's sugar consumption would rise by 190,000 tonnes to 1.11 million tonnes.
South Africa's production from October 1995 to Septmeber 1996 amounted to 2.34 million tonnes, compared with the 2.21 previously reported, the ISO said.
In the northern hemisphere, the ISO further reduced its estimate for Indian production by 150,000 tonnes to 15.35 million tonnes.
But Thailand was still expected to turn out record production of 6.40 million tonnes compared with 6.32 million in 1995/96.
In the southern hemisphere, the damage caused by cyclone Justin could limit the 1997 production growth in Australia to 5.43 million tonnes.
This compared with the 5.70 million estimated previously and the 5.35 million produced in the 1995/96 Oct/Sept cycle.
Brazil's production estimated was upgraded by 600,000 tonnes to 14.1 million tonnes after 14.63 in 1995/96.
In Cuba, the ISO said current indications were that the cane crop would beonly slightly better than last year's 4.5 million tonnes. It maintained its estaimte of 4.8 million tonnes.
The ISO said its fourth assessment of the world 1996/97 sugar balance showed ending stocks at 40.97 million tonnes, 409,000 tonnes or 1.00 percent up from the previous season.
The European Union was expected to see a stock increase of 550,000 tonnes, it said.

"World export availability is expected to exceed import demand by 1.88 million tonnes in 1996/97," the ISO said, adding that exportable -- but unsold -- sugar could be added to the new season's beginning stocks.

"This pessimistic but realistic scenario would make the stocks at the beginning of the forthcoming 1997/98 crop cycle as high as 42.8 million tonnes, or 35 percent of this crop year world consumption."
